      No clear winner in Israel as exit polls suggest rebuke for Netanyahu
    

  
    
        PM's rival Gadi Eisenkot says Israelis voted for change, as polls show neither side has a majority

Inconclusive Israeli election leaves future leadership uncertain

        Netanyahu's party loses seats, but nobody has an outright majority yet. Here's the latest
            
                  
        
              
                
              
        
        
          By Jessie Yeung
        


            
    
    
        
                
      
    
       
    
    
    
      
        
        
    
    Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
    
  
        Getty Images
      
    


    
            It’s the early hours of Wednesday morning in Israel, and the election – one of the most consequential in years – is over. Now begins the real work of counting votes and forming a government.

It’ll take several days to finalize the vote count, but exit polls indicate Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party has taken a blow – though there’s not yet a clear winner with an outright majority.

Link Copied!
        
    
    
        

    
    
        

    


    
    
        Arab voters turn out in record numbers but entering government will still be tricky
            
                  
        
              
                
              
              
                
              
        
        
          By Zeena Saifi and Kathleen Magramo
        


            
    
    
        
                
      
    
       
    
    
    
      
        
        
    
    Supporters of Israel's Arab-led Joint List political alliance cheer at its campaign headquarters in the northern Israeli city of Nazareth on Tuesday, as the first exit polls are announced on television.
    
  
        Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images
      
    


    
            Supporters of Israel’s Arab Joint List party celebrated at its election headquarters in Nazareth, with Arab parties projected to gain a record number of seats from Tuesday’s election.

Party leader Yousef Jabareen commended a strong turnout among the community, saying it was “unprecedented and historic in our Arab society.” Arab voters make up about 20% of the Israeli electorate, but have traditionally voted at lower rates than Jewish Israelis.

That voter surge was driven by an urgent desire to dismantle Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition, which includes hardline ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.

That sentiment was underscored by chants of “Ben-Gvir, go home” at the Joint List election headquarters.

Jabareen said exit polls showed Arab-led parties can “make a difference.”

He vowed to be a “safety net in the face of crime in our society, a safety net in the face of dangerous racism, a safety net in the face of the demolition of homes and entire villages.”

Context: Entering government could still be tricky for Arab parties. Between them, the Joint List and Raam are projected to secure 17-19 seats in the 120-seat Knessett, their strongest showing in history.

Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party is projected to win 21-23 seats.

However, Eisenkot has set conditions for any partner to join his government, including recognizing Israel as a Jewish state and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization that must be dismantled, terms most Arab lawmakers are unlikely to accept.

Moreover, two of his opposition allies – Avigdor Lieberman and Naftali Bennett – have ruled out forming a government with the Arab parties altogether.

Link Copied!
        
    
    
        

    
    
        

    


    
    
        Trump says he hasn't spoken to Netanyahu, but heard "he's doing pretty well"
            
                  
        
              
                
              
        
        
          By Jessie Yeung
        


            
    
    
        
                    
            US President Donald Trump said early Wednesday he hadn’t yet spoken to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but seemed optimistic about his performance in the election as the vote count is underway.

“I’m hearing that he did very well, and it’s pretty close,” he said, speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

Just over a week before the polls opened in Israel, Trump called Netanyahu a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” in a Truth Social post, offering his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”

Exit polls so far suggest Netanyahu’s bloc lost its majority in the Knesset – though it is narrowly in the lead over the opposition. Trump suggested that the exit polls might be wrong, however.

“He might be winning, or tied,” he said. “It’s a little bit early, but I’m hearing that in Israel, top people are saying, ‘Wow,’ he did a lot better than people thought.”

The final result could be “a stalemate or a win – but we’ll find out,” he added.

Link Copied!
        
    
    
        

    
    
        

    


    
    
        After a critical election, the ultimate outcome will take time to become clear
            
                  
        
              
                
              
        
        
          By Tal Shalev
        


            
    
    
        
                    
            Israel’s elections produced no clear winner Tuesday night, exit polls showed, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot within reach of the 61 seats needed for a governing majority in the 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.

The three main Israeli TV Channels – 11, 12 and 13 – projected Netanyahu’s bloc at 51-52 seats, marking a steep drop from the 68-seat coalition he led in the outgoing Knesset. His Likud party is still projected to be the largest party, with 25-27 seats.

But Israeli politics is all about building coalitions – not being the biggest party – and Netanyahu’s path to staying in power is now unclear.

Link Copied!
        
    
    
        

    
    
        

    


    
    
        Why exit poll numbers are only part of the story in Israel’s election
            
                  
        
        
        
          By Oren Liebermann
        


            
    
    
        
                    
            The release of the exit polls is a key moment that gives the first indications of what the results may be as the polls close. But they are only exit polls, trying to approximate a final result with imperfect information.

And as we saw very early Wednesday morning, they can be wrong.

The initial results projected that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc slightly trailed the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot. But in the ensuing hours, Netanyahu’s bloc either tied or slightly surpassed Eisenkot’s. He also opened up a gap between the two individual parties, with his Likud several seats ahead of Eisenkot’s Yashar.

Crucially, neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot declared outright victory. Both men projected strength and a path forward but stopped short of saying they had won. They simply don’t know if they had.

As the official vote count gets underway, the exit polls become less relevant. Now, the Israeli public is waiting on real results. Those are expected sometime late Wednesday or early Thursday. And it will take several more days to officially certify the results.

So why does anyone pay attention to the exit polls at all? Because they give the first indication of what the results may be. It’s just not always the right results.

Link Copied!
        
    
    
        

    
    
        

    


    
    
        Eisenkot supporters' desire to oust Netanyahu outweighs traditional alliances
            
                  
        
              
                
              
        
        
          By Florence Davey-Attlee and Avi Halfon in Tel Aviv
        


            
    
    
        
                
      
    
       
    
    
    
      
        
        
    
    Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar ("Straight") party, waves to supporters following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election in Tel Aviv, Israel, on October 28.
    
  
        Baz Ratner/AP
      
    


    
            As election results began trickling in late Tuesday, Gadi Eisenkot supporters who had gathered at the Yashar party campaign headquarters expressed an openness to aligning with Arab parties to form a government.

For these voters, their desire to unseat Netanyahu outweighs anything else.

Among them were Yigal and Racheli Raz, who emphasized their vote for Eisenkot was a vote for change.

“We are sure that Gadi will do what will be the best for our country, and if it will be that we connect with the Arabs, so that’s it,” Yigal said.

Racheli said co-operation with Arab parties was “not a deal breaker” if it meant Israel could have a new government. “We have to make a change in Israel, we have to,” she said. “We can’t stand it any more.”

“We will prefer that he will connect with other Zionist parties, but if it doesn’t succeed, there is always another option, and that option will be to somehow to connect with the Arab parties and to make change,” Yigal said, adding: “What we are saying is that we trust Gadi, that he will do what’s the best for our country.”

For context: Neither Netanyahu’s right wing bloc or the Eisenkot-led opposition bloc can reach a 61-seat majority on their own. Meanwhile, Arab parties, are forecast to win a record 19 seats according to exit polls. Netanyahu’s bloc will not cooperate with the Arab parties; several figures in the opposition bloc have also ruled out cooperation.

Link Copied!
        
    
    
        

    
    
        

    


    
    
        Exit polls shift slightly to Netanyahu, but he’s still well short of a majority
            
                  
        
              
                
              
        
        
          By Dana Karni and Oren Liebermann
        


            
    
    
        
                    
            Exit polls from Israel’s three main pollsters shifted slightly toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, putting him tied with or slightly ahead of the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.

Israel’s Channel 12 News put Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing and ultra-Orthodox parties at 52 seats, according to its latest update to the exit polls, while the Eisenkot-led bloc dropped to 49 seats. The Arab parties strengthened by one to 19 seats.

The poll also suggested Netanyahu’s Likud party opened up a lead over Eisenkot’s Yashar party, 27 seats to 21 seats.

But Netanyahu is still well short of a majority of 61 seats needed to declare victory, the exit poll still indicated. Eisenkot is also short of an outright majority, needing to cooperate with the Arab parties in order to oust Israel’s longest-serving leader.

Both Channel 13 and Channel 11 News found in their exit polls that the Netanyahu bloc was tied with Eisenkot’s bloc at 51 seats apiece. The Arab parties held 18 seats, the polls indicated.

        Netanyahu thanks Trump, and God, for making him Israel's leader
            
                  
        
              
                
              
        
        
          By Jessie Yeung
        


            
    
    
        
                
      
    
       
    
    
    
      
        
        
    
    Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addresses his supporters after the first exit polls were announced, in Jerusalem on early October 28, during Israel's legislative elections.
    
  
        Jewel Samad/AFP/Getty Images
      
    


    
            Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked many of his supporters in his speech early Wednesday, among whom he counted US President Donald Trump and God.

“Together with our great friend President Trump, we are determined to eliminate this threat once and for all,” he said, referring to Iran and the ongoing war.

He also thanked members of his Likud party, other government and coalition partners, his wife and children, and Israel’s soldiers.

“Finally I’d like to thank the creator of the world, which is giving me the power to continue to act for the eternity of Israel and our beloved nation and state – our only state,” he said at the end of his speech.
